title: Closed Form for Triangular Numbers
theorem_text:
The closed-form expression for the $n$th triangular number is:
$\displaystyle T_n = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2$
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
Basis for the Induction
When $n = 1$, we have:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^1 i = 1$
Also:
$\dfrac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2 = \dfrac {1 \cdot 2} 2 = 1$
This is our base case.
Induction Hypothesis
$\forall k \in \N: k \ge 1: \displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i = \frac {k \paren {k + 1} } 2$
This is our induction hypothesis.
It is to be demonstrated that:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i = \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {k + 2} } 2$
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
Consider $n = k + 1$.
By the properties of summation:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i + k + 1$
Using the induction hypothesis this can be simplified to:
$$\frac {k \paren {k + 1} } 2 + k + 1 = \frac {k \paren {k + 1} + 2 k + 2} 2$$
$$= \frac {k^2 + 3 k + 2} 2$$
$$= \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {k + 2} } 2$$
$$= \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {\paren {k + 1} + 1} } 2$$
Hence the result by induction.
review_reason: The base case holds. For an arbitrary k the step uses only the formula at k, adds k+1, and factors the resulting expression. The universal quantifier in the hypothesis line is unnecessary for that argument.

title: Closed Form for Triangular Numbers
theorem_text:
The closed-form expression for the $n$th triangular number is:
$\displaystyle T_n = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2$
proof_text:
Triangular numbers are $k$-gonal numbers where $k = 3$.
From Closed Form for Polygonal Numbers we have that:
$P \left({k, n}\right) = \dfrac n 2 \left({\left({k - 2}\right) n - k + 4}\right)$
Hence:
$$T_n = \frac n 2 \left({\left({3 - 2}\right) n - 3 + 4}\right)$$
Closed Form for Polygonal Numbers
$$= \frac n 2 \left({n + 1}\right)$$
Hence the result.
review_reason: Triangular numbers are the k=3 instance of the cited polygonal-number formula. Substituting 3 gives n(n+1)/2.

title: Sum of Sequence of Squares
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \forall n \in \N: \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^2 = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6$
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
For all $n \in \N$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^2 = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6$
When $n = 0$, we see from the definition of vacuous sum that:
$0 = \displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^0 i^2 = \frac {0 \paren 1 \paren 1} 6 = 0$
and so $\map P 0$ holds.
Basis for the Induction
When $n = 1$:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^1 i^2 = 1^2 = 1$
Now, we have:
$\displaystyle \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6 = \frac {1 \paren {1 + 1} \paren {2 \times 1 + 1} } 6 = \frac 6 6 = 1$
and $\map P 1$ is seen to hold.
This is our basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now we need to show that, if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is our induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i^2 = \frac {k \paren {k + 1} \paren {2 k + 1} } 6$
Then we need to show:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^2 = \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {k + 2} \paren {2 \paren {k + 1} + 1} } 6$
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
Using the properties of summation, we have:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^2 = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i^2 + \paren {k + 1}^2$
We can now apply our induction hypothesis, obtaining:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^2 = \frac {k \paren {k + 1} \paren {2 k + 1} } 6 + \paren {k + 1}^2$$
$$= \frac {k \paren {k + 1} \paren {2 k + 1} + 6 \paren {k + 1}^2} 6$$
$$= \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {k \paren {2 k + 1} + 6 \paren {k + 1} } } 6$$
$$= \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {2 k^2 + 7 k + 6} } 6$$
$$= \frac {\paren {k + 1} \paren {k + 2} \paren {2 \paren {k + 1} + 1} } 6$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \forall n \in \N: \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^2 = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6$
review_reason: The proof checks the empty sum and the first positive case. Adding (k+1)^2 to the induction hypothesis gives (k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)/6.

title: Sum of Sequence of Squares
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \forall n \in \N: \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^2 = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6$
proof_text:
Observe that:
$3 i \left({i + 1}\right) = i \left({i + 1}\right) \left({i + 2}\right) - i \left({i + 1}\right) \left({i - 1}\right)$
That is:
$(1): \quad 6 T_i = \left({i + 1}\right) \left({\left({i + 1}\right) + 1}\right) \left({\left({i + 1}\right) - 1}\right) - i \left({i + 1}\right) \left({i - 1}\right)$
Then:
$$n^2 = \frac {n^2 + n + n^2 - n} 2$$
$$= \frac {n \left({n + 1}\right) + n \left({n - 1}\right)} 2$$
$$= \frac {n \left({n + 1}\right)} 2 + \frac {n \left({n - 1}\right)} 2$$
$$= T_n + T_{n-1}$$
where $T_n$ is the $n$th Triangular number.
Then:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^2 = 1 + \left({T_1 + T_2}\right) + \left({T_2 + T_3}\right) + \left({T_3 + T_4}\right) + \cdots + \left({T_{n - 1} + T_n}\right)$$
$$= 1 + 2 T_2 + 2 T_3 + 2 T_4 + \cdots + 2 T_{n - 1} + T_n$$
$$= 1 - T_1 - T_n + 2 \left({T_1 + T_2 + T_3 + T_4 + \cdots + T_n}\right)$$
$$= 2 \left({\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n T_i} \right) - \frac {n \left({n + 1}\right)} 2$$
$$= 2 \left({\frac {n \left({n + 1}\right) \left({n + 2}\right)} 6}\right) - \frac {n \left({n + 1}\right)} 2$$
Telescoping Series from $(1)$ above
$$= \frac {2 n \left({n^2 + 3 n + 2}\right) - \left({3 n^2 + 3 n}\right)} 6$$
$$= \frac {2 n^3 + 3 n^2 + n} 6$$
$$= \frac {n \left({n + 1}\right) \left({2 n + 1}\right)} 6$$
review_reason: The regrouping loses one copy of T_1. For n=3 the sum is 1+(1+3)+(3+6)=14, but the next displayed expression is 1+2(3)+6=13. The later correct formula does not make that equality true.

title: Square Root of Prime is Irrational
theorem_text: The square root of any prime number is irrational.
proof_text:
Let $p \in \Z$ be a prime number.
Consider the polynomial:
$\map P x = x^2 - p$
over the ring of polynomials $\Q \sqbrk X$ over the rational numbers.
From Difference of Two Squares:
$x^2 - p = \paren {x + \sqrt p} \paren {x + \sqrt p}$
Because $p$ is prime, $\sqrt p$ is not an integer.
From Polynomial which is Irreducible over Integers is Irreducible over Rationals it follows that $\paren {x + \sqrt p}$ and $\paren {x + \sqrt p}$ do not have rational coefficients.
That is:
$\sqrt p$ is not rational.
Hence the result.
review_reason: The claimed factorization uses x+sqrt(p) twice. Already at x=0 its product equals p, whereas x^2-p equals -p. The subsequent argument relies on this false factorization.

title: Derivative of Sine Function
theorem_text: $\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\sin x} = \cos x$
proof_text:
From the definition of the sine function, we have:
$\displaystyle \sin x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {x^{2 n + 1} } {\paren {2 n + 1}!}$
From Radius of Convergence of Power Series over Factorial, this series converges for all $x$.
From Power Series is Differentiable on Interval of Convergence:
$$\map {\frac \d {\d x} } {\sin x} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {x^{2 n + 1} } {\paren {2 n + 1}!}$$
$$= \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {x^{2 n} } {\paren {2 n}!}$$
The result follows from the definition of the cosine function.
review_reason: The first displayed derivative is set equal to the original sine series with all exponents unchanged. At x=0 that series equals 0 and the next displayed cosine series equals 1. The first equality would need a differentiation operator.

title: Derivative of Sine Function
theorem_text: $\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\sin x} = \cos x$
proof_text:
$$\dfrac \d {\d x} \sin x = \dfrac \d {\d x} \map \cos {\frac \pi 2 - x}$$
Cosine of Complement equals Sine
$$= \map \sin {\frac \pi 2 - x}$$
Derivative of Cosine Function and Chain Rule for Derivatives
$$= \cos x$$
Sine of Complement equals Cosine
review_reason: Differentiating cos(pi/2-x) introduces two minus signs, which cancel. The cofunction identity then gives cos(x).

proof_text:
By Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence:
$0.999 \ldots = \dfrac a {1 - r}$
where $a = \dfrac 9 {10}$ and $r = \dfrac 1 {10}$.
Since our ratio is less than $1$, then we know that $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac 9 {10} \paren {\frac 1 {10} }^n$ must converge to:
$\dfrac a {1 - r} = \dfrac {\frac 9 {10} } {1 - \frac 1 {10} } = \dfrac {\frac 9 {10} } {\frac 9 {10} } = 1$
review_reason: The recurring decimal is the geometric series with first term 9/10 and ratio 1/10. The ratio has absolute value less than 1, and the sum is 1.

proof_text:
We begin with the knowledge that:
$$\frac 9 9 = \frac 1 1 = 1$$
Now we divide $9$ by $9$ using the standard process of long division, only instead of stating that $90$ divided by $9$ is $10$, we say that it is "$9$ remainder $9$," yielding the following result:
$
\require{enclose}
\phantom{0..}0.9999\ldots\\
9\enclose{longdiv}{9.0000\ldots}\\
\phantom{0}\underline{\phantom{0}8.1}\\
\phantom{000.}90\\
\phantom{0.}\underline{\phantom{00}81}\\
\phantom{0000.}90\\
\phantom{0.}\underline{\phantom{000}81}\\
\phantom{00000.}9\ldots\\
$
Thus, we are compelled to believe that:
$0.999\ldots = \dfrac 9 9 = 1$
review_reason: The nonstandard quotient digit is justified by 90=9·9+9 at each repetition. After k digits the scaled unaccounted portion of the quotient is 10^(-k), which tends to zero. Thus these digits do represent 9/9.

title: Sum of Sequence of Cubes
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i}^2 = \frac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
proof_text:
First, from Closed Form for Triangular Numbers:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i = \frac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2$
So:
$\displaystyle \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i}^2 = \dfrac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
Next we use induction on $n$ to show that:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \dfrac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $n \in \Z_{>0}$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \dfrac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 1$ is the case:
$1^3 = \dfrac {1 \paren {1 + 1}^2} 4$
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^1 i^3 = 1^3$$
$$= \dfrac {1^2 \paren {1 + 1}^2} 4$$
Thus $\map P 1$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i^3 = \dfrac {k^2 \paren {k + 1}^2} 4$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^3 = \dfrac {\paren {k + 1}^2 \paren {k + 2}^2} 4$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^3 = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i^3 + \paren {k + 1}^3$$
$$= \frac {k^2 \paren {k + 1}^2} 4 + \paren {k + 1}^3$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= \frac {k^4 + 2 k^3 + k^2} 4 + \frac {4 k^3 + 12 k^2 + 12 k + 4} 4$$
$$= \frac {k^4 + 6 k^3 + 13 k^2 + 12 k + 4} 4$$
$$= \frac {\paren {k + 1}^2 \paren {k + 2}^2} 4$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\forall n \in \Z_{>0}: \displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \dfrac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
review_reason: The triangular-number formula supplies the squared-sum expression. Starting at 1, adding (k+1)^3 produces (k+1)^2(k+2)^2/4 as required.

title: Sum of Sequence of Cubes
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i}^2 = \frac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
proof_text:
By Nicomachus's Theorem, we have:
$\forall n \in \N_{>0}: n^3 = \left({n^2 - n + 1}\right) + \paren {n^2 - n + 3} + \ldots + \paren {n^2 + n - 1}$
Also by Nicomachus's Theorem, we have that the first term for $\paren {n + 1}^3$ is $2$ greater than the last term for $n^3$.
So if we add them all up together, we get:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \sum_{\stackrel {1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n^2 \mathop + n \mathop - 1} {i \text { odd} } } i$$
... the sum of all the odd numbers up to $n^2 + n - 1$
$$= \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{\frac {n^2 \mathop + n} 2} 2 i - 1$$
... that is, the first $\dfrac {n^2 + n} 2$ odd numbers
$$= \paren {\frac {n^2 + n} 2}^2$$
Odd Number Theorem
Hence the result.
review_reason: The cited identity expresses successive cubes as consecutive blocks of odd numbers with no gaps. The last odd number is n(n+1)-1, giving n(n+1)/2 odd summands and hence the stated square.

title: Sum of Sequence of Cubes
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i}^2 = \frac {n^2 \paren {n + 1}^2} 4$
proof_text:
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $n \in \Z_{> 0}$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = {T_n}^2$
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 1$ is the case:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^1 i^3 = 1^3$$
$$= 1$$
$$= \paren {\frac {1 \paren {1 + 1} } 2}^2$$
$$= {T_1}^2$$
Closed Form for Triangular Numbers
Thus $\map P 1$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that, if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 2$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i^3 = {T_k}^2$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^3 = {T_{k + 1} }^2$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} i^3 = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k i^3 + \paren {k + 1}^3$$
$$= {T_k}^2 + \paren {k + 1}^3$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= {T_k}^2 + \paren { {T_{k + 1} }^2 - {T_k}^2}$$
Cube Number as Difference between Squares of Triangular Numbers
$$= {T_{k + 1} }^2$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\forall n \in \Z_{> 0}: \displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^3 = {T_n}^2$
review_reason: The cited difference of consecutive triangular squares equals (k+1)^3. This gives the step for every k≥1, including k=1, despite the introductory line stating k≥2. The base case and displayed step therefore suffice.

title: Lagrange's Theorem (Group Theory)
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a finite group.
Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.
Then:
$\order H$ divides $\order G$
where $\order G$ and $\order H$ are the order of $G$ and $H$ respectively.
In fact:
$\index G H = \dfrac {\order G} {\order H}$
where $\index G H$ is the index of $H$ in $G$.
When $G$ is an infinite group, we can still interpret this theorem sensibly:
:A subgroup of finite index in an infinite group is itself an infinite group.
:A finite subgroup of an infinite group has infinite index.
proof_text:
Let $G$ be a group.
Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.
From Cosets are Equivalent, a left coset $y H$ has the same number of elements as $H$, namely $\order H$.
Since left cosets are identical or disjoint, each element of $G$ belongs to exactly one left coset.
From the definition of index of subgroup, there are $\index G H$ left cosets, and therefore:
$\order G = \index G H \order H$
Let $G$ be of finite order.
All three numbers are finite, and the result follows.
Now let $G$ be of infinite order.
If $\index G H = n$ is finite, then $\order G = n \order H$ and so $H$ is of infinite order.
If $H$ is of finite order such that $\order H = n$, then $\order G = \index G H \times n$ and so $\index G H$ is infinite.
review_reason: The cosets partition G into sets equipotent to H. Counting gives the finite order formula. If both the index and subgroup order were finite, G would be a finite union of finite cosets, proving both infinite-group assertions.

title: Lagrange's Theorem (Group Theory)
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a finite group.
Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.
Then:
$\order H$ divides $\order G$
where $\order G$ and $\order H$ are the order of $G$ and $H$ respectively.
In fact:
$\index G H = \dfrac {\order G} {\order H}$
where $\index G H$ is the index of $H$ in $G$.
When $G$ is an infinite group, we can still interpret this theorem sensibly:
:A subgroup of finite index in an infinite group is itself an infinite group.
:A finite subgroup of an infinite group has infinite index.
proof_text:
Let $G$ be finite.
Consider the mapping $\phi: G \to G / H^l$, defined as:
$\phi: G \to G / H^l: \map \phi x = x H^l$
where $G / H^l$ is the left coset space of $G$ modulo $H$.
For every $y H \in G / H^l$, there exists a corresponding $y \in G$, so $\phi$ is a surjection.
From Cardinality of Surjection it follows that $G / H^l$ is finite.
From Cosets are Equivalent, $G / H^l$ has the same number of elements as $H$.
We have that the $G / H^l$ is a partition of $G$.
It follows from Number of Elements in Partition that $\index G H = \dfrac {\order G} {\order H}$
review_reason: Coset equipotence gives |yH|=|H| for each coset. The proof applies it to the entire coset space and asserts |G/H|=|H|, which already fails for a trivial subgroup of a nontrivial finite group.

title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
theorem_text: For every integer $n$ such that $n > 1$, $n$ can be expressed as the product of one or more primes, uniquely up to the order in which they appear.
proof_text:
In Integer is Expressible as Product of Primes it is proved that every integer $n$ such that $n > 1$, $n$ can be expressed as the product of one or more primes.
In Prime Decomposition of Integer is Unique, it is proved that this prime decomposition is unique up to the order of the factors.
review_reason: The two cited results establish exactly the two required clauses for integers greater than 1: existence of a prime factorization and uniqueness up to reordering.

title: Integers form Unique Factorization Domain
theorem_text: The integers $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ form a unique factorization domain.
proof_text:
Follows directly from:
$(1) \quad$ the fundamental theorem of arithmetic
$(2) \quad$ the fact that $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ is an integral domain
$(3) \quad$ the definitions complete factorization and equivalent factorizations.
review_reason: The fundamental theorem of arithmetic gives existence and uniqueness for positive integers above one. The units account for signs, giving uniqueness up to associates and order in the integer domain.

title: Euclid's Lemma
theorem_text:
Let $a, b, c \in \Z$.
Let $a \divides b c$, where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Let $a \perp b$, where $\perp$ denotes relative primeness.
Then $a \divides c$.
proof_text:
We have that the integers form a Euclidean domain.
Then from Irreducible Elements of Ring of Integers we have that the irreducible elements of $\Z$ are the primes and their negatives.
The result then follows directly from Euclid's Lemma for Irreducible Elements.
review_reason: The cited lemma applies to an irreducible divisor. The theorem allows composite a, such as 12. Identifying the irreducibles of the integers does not extend that lemma to arbitrary coprime divisors or account for their prime multiplicities.

title: Euclid's Lemma
theorem_text:
Let $a, b, c \in \Z$.
Let $a \divides b c$, where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Let $a \perp b$, where $\perp$ denotes relative primeness.
Then $a \divides c$.
proof_text:
Let $p \divides a b$.
Suppose $p \nmid a$.
Then from the definition of prime:
$p \perp a$
where $\perp$ indicates that $p$ and $a$ are coprime.
Thus from Euclid's Lemma it follows that:
$p \divides b$
Similarly, if $p \nmid b$ it follows that $p \divides a$.
So:
$p \divides a b \implies p \divides a$ or $p \divides b$
as we needed to show.
review_reason: The argument treats the divisor p as prime when it infers coprimality from nondivisibility. The stated divisor may be composite. It then invokes Euclid's lemma itself to prove a different, prime-divisor assertion.

title: Euclid's Lemma
theorem_text:
Let $a, b, c \in \Z$.
Let $a \divides b c$, where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Let $a \perp b$, where $\perp$ denotes relative primeness.
Then $a \divides c$.
proof_text:
Let $a, b, c \in \Z$.
We have that $a \perp b$.
That is:
$\gcd \set {a, b} = 1$
where $\gcd$ denotes greatest common divisor.
From Bézout's Lemma, we may write:
$a x + b y = 1$
for some $x, y \in \Z$.
Upon multiplication by $c$, we see that:
$c = c \paren {a x + b y} = c a x + c b y$
Now note that $c a x + c b y$ is an integer combination of $a c$ and $b c$.
So, since:
$a \divides a c$
and:
$a \divides b c$
it follows from Common Divisor Divides Integer Combination that:
$a \divides \paren {c a x + c b y}$
However:
$c a x + c b y = c \paren {a x + b y} = c \cdot 1 = c$
Therefore:
$a \divides c$
review_reason: Multiplying Bézout's identity ax+by=1 by c expresses c as an integer combination of ac and bc. Both are divisible by a under the hypotheses.

title: Fermat's Little Theorem
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer such that $p$ is not a divisor of $n$.
Then:
$n^{p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$
proof_text:
By Prime not Divisor implies Coprime:
$p \nmid n \implies p \perp n$
and Euler's Theorem can be applied.
Thus:
$n^{\map \phi p} \equiv 1 \pmod p$
But from Euler Phi Function of Prime Power:
$\map \phi p = p \paren {1 - \dfrac 1 p} = p - 1$
and the result follows.
review_reason: Since p is prime and does not divide n, n is a unit modulo p. Euler's theorem applies and phi(p)=p-1 gives the specified exponent.

title: Fermat's Little Theorem
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer such that $p$ is not a divisor of $n$.
Then:
$n^{p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$
proof_text:
Let $\struct {\Z'_p, \times}$ denote the multiplicative group of reduced residues modulo $p$.
From the corollary to Reduced Residue System under Multiplication forms Abelian Group, $\struct {\Z'_p, \times}$ forms a group of order $p - 1$ under modulo multiplication.
By Element to Power of Group Order is Identity, we have:
$n^{p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$
review_reason: The class of n is in the multiplicative group of nonzero residues because p does not divide n. Raising a group element to the group order p-1 gives the identity.

title: Fermat's Little Theorem
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer such that $p$ is not a divisor of $n$.
Then:
$n^{p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$
proof_text:
Proof by induction over $n$.
Induction base:
$1^p \equiv 1 \pmod p$
Induction step:
Assume $n^p \equiv n \pmod p$
$$\paren {n + 1}^p = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^p {p \choose k} n^{p - k} \cdot 1^k$$
Binomial Theorem
$$\forall k: 0 < k < p: {p \choose k} \equiv 0 \pmod p$$
Binomial Coefficient of Prime
and so:
$$\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^p {p \choose k} n^{p - k} \equiv n^p + n^0 \pmod p$$
$$\equiv n^p + 1 \pmod p$$
$$\equiv n + 1 \pmod p$$
by induction step
Dividing by $n$:
$\forall n: n^p \equiv n \pmod p \implies n^{p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$
review_reason: The interior binomial coefficients vanish modulo p, so the induction proves n^p≡n. For the n in the theorem, p does not divide n, which justifies the final modular cancellation.

title: 1+2+...+n+(n-1)+...+1 = n^2
theorem_text: $\forall n \in \N: 1 + 2 + \cdots + n + \paren {n - 1} + \cdots + 1 = n^2$
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
Basis for the Induction
$n = 1$ holds trivially.
Just to make sure, we try $n = 2$:
$1 + 2 + 1 = 4$
Likewise $n^2 = 2^2 = 4$.
So shown for basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
This is our induction hypothesis:
$1 + 2 + \cdots + k + \paren {k - 1} + \cdots + 1 = k^2$
Now we need to show true for $n = k + 1$:
$1 + 2 + \cdots + \paren {k + 1} + k + \paren {k - 1} + \cdots + 1 = \paren {k + 1}^2$
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
$$1 + 2 + \cdots + \paren {k + 1} + k + \paren {k - 1} + \cdots + 1$$
$$= \paren {1 + 2 + \cdots + k + \paren {k - 1} + \cdots + 1} + k + \paren {k + 1}$$
$$= k^2 + k + \paren {k + 1}$$
from induction hypothesis
$$= k^2 + 2k + 1$$
$$= \paren {k + 1}^2$$
The result follows by induction.
review_reason: From the expression with peak k to the one with peak k+1 the added terms total k+(k+1). Adding them to k² gives (k+1)², with the initial peak 1 verified.

title: Odd Number Theorem
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \paren {2 j - 1} = n^2$
That is, the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is the $n$th square number.
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
For all $n \in \N_{>0}$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle n^2 = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \paren {2 j - 1}$
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 1$ is true, as this just says $1^2 = 1$.
This is our basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now we need to show that, if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is our induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle k^2 = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k \paren {2 j - 1}$
Then we need to show:
$\displaystyle \paren {k + 1}^2 = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} \paren {2 j - 1}$
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
$$\paren {k + 1}^2 = k^2 + 2 k + 1$$
$$= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k \paren {2 j - 1} + 2 k + 1$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k \paren {2 j - 1} + 2 \paren {k + 1} - 1$$
$$= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} \paren {2 j - 1}$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \forall n \in \N: n^2 = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \paren {2 j - 1}$
review_reason: Adding the next odd term 2k+1 changes the inductive sum from k squared to (k+1) squared. The empty sum also gives the zero case.

title: Sum of Consecutive Triangular Numbers is Square
theorem_text: The sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is a square number.
proof_text:
Let $T_{n - 1}$ and $T_n$ be two consecutive triangular numbers.
From Closed Form for Triangular Numbers, we have:
$T_{n - 1} = \dfrac {\paren {n - 1} n} 2$
$T_n = \dfrac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2$
So:
$$T_{n - 1} + T_n = \frac {\paren {n - 1} n} 2 + \frac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2$$
$$= \frac {\paren {n - 1 + n + 1} n} 2$$
$$= \frac {2 n^2} 2$$
$$= n^2$$
review_reason: Adding the two consecutive triangular-number formulas cancels the linear terms and gives n squared.

title: Existence of Rational Powers of Irrational Numbers
theorem_text: There exist irrational numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $a^b$ is rational.
proof_text:
We have that:
$\sqrt 2$ is irrational.
$2$ is trivially rational, as $2 = \dfrac 2 1$.
Consider the number $q = \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}$, which is irrational by the Gelfond-Schneider Theorem.
Thus:
$q^{\sqrt 2} = \left({\sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}}\right)^{\sqrt 2} = \sqrt 2 ^{\left({\sqrt 2}\right) \left({\sqrt 2}\right)} = \sqrt 2^2 = 2$
is rational.
So $a = q = \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}$ and $b = \sqrt 2$ are the desired irrationals.
review_reason: Gelfond–Schneider applies because sqrt(2) is algebraic, different from 0 and 1, and the exponent sqrt(2) is algebraic irrational. The resulting positive irrational base raised to sqrt(2) gives 2.

title: Existence of Rational Powers of Irrational Numbers
theorem_text: There exist irrational numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $a^b$ is rational.
proof_text:
Given that $2$ is rational and $\sqrt 2$ is irrational, consider the number $q = \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}$.
We consider the two cases.
$(1): \quad$ If $q$ is rational then $a = \sqrt 2$ and $b = \sqrt 2$ are the desired irrational numbers.
$(2): \quad$ If $q$ is irrational then $q^{\sqrt 2} = \paren {\sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} }^{\sqrt 2} = \sqrt 2^{\paren {\sqrt 2} \paren {\sqrt 2} } = \sqrt 2^2 = 2$ is rational, so $a = q = \sqrt2^{\sqrt 2}$ and $b = \sqrt 2$ are the desired irrational numbers.
review_reason: The rational and irrational cases for q exhaust the possibilities. They supply respectively the witness pairs (sqrt(2),sqrt(2)) and (q,sqrt(2)), and both powers are rational.

title: Existence of Rational Powers of Irrational Numbers
theorem_text: There exist irrational numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $a^b$ is rational.
proof_text:
Consider the equation:
$\left({\sqrt 2}\right)^{\log_{\sqrt 2} 3} = 3$
We have that $\sqrt 2$ is irrational and $3$ is (trivially) rational.
It remains to be proved $\log_{\sqrt 2} 3$ is irrational.
We have:
$$\log_{\sqrt 2} 3 = \frac{\log_2 3}{\log_2 \sqrt 2}$$
Change of Base of Logarithm
$$= \frac{\log_2 3}{1/2}$$
Logarithms of Powers: $\sqrt 2 = 2^{1/2}$ and $\log_2 2 = 1$
$$= 2 \, \log_2 3$$
From Irrationality of Logarithm, $\log_2 3$ is irrational.
Therefore $2 \, \log_2 3$ is irrational.
Thus there exist two irrational numbers $a = \sqrt 2$ and $b = \log_{\sqrt 2} 3$ such that $a^b$ is rational.
review_reason: Change of base gives log base sqrt(2) of 3 as twice log base 2 of 3, an irrational number by the cited logarithm result. The defining exponential identity gives the rational value 3.

title: Empty Set is Unique
theorem_text: The empty set is unique.
proof_text:
Let $\O$ and $\O'$ both be empty sets.
From Empty Set is Subset of All Sets, $\O \subseteq \O'$, because $\O$ is empty.
Likewise, we have $\O' \subseteq \O$, since $\O'$ is empty.
Together, by the definition of set equality, this implies that $\O = \O'$.
Thus there is only one empty set.
review_reason: Each empty set is a subset of the other by vacuity. Mutual inclusion gives equality by extensionality.

title: Empty Set is Unique
theorem_text: The empty set is unique.
proof_text:
Let $A$ and $B$ both be empty sets.
Thus:
$\forall x: \neg \paren {x \in A}$
and:
$\forall x: \neg \paren {x \in B}$
Hence:
$x \notin A \iff x \notin B$
and so:
$x \in A \iff x \in B$
vacuously.
From Axiom of Extension:
$\forall x: \paren {x \in A \iff x \in B} \iff A = B$
Hence the result.
review_reason: Every object fails membership in both sets, giving identical membership predicates. Extensionality then gives equality.
